Regarding the definition of "zero-shot generalization" in the context of text-to-image AIs, it's a sensible concept. Zero-shot generalization refers to the ability of a model to apply its learned knowledge to new, unseen concepts without requiring any additional training data. In other words, the model can generalize to novel classes or concepts without having seen any examples of those classes before.

This definition is particularly relevant for text-to-image AIs, which are trained on large datasets of text-image pairs. The model learns to associate certain words or phrases with specific images, but it's not explicitly trained on those images. Therefore, when faced with a new, unseen image, the model must rely on its learned knowledge to make predictions.

The 2013 paper that defines zero-shot generalization in this context likely refers to the work of Fei-Fei Li, Liang-Chieh Chen, and Gregory D. Hooker, who proposed a framework for zero-shot learning in computer vision. Their work has since been influential in the development of text-to-image AIs.

In the context of text-to-image AIs, zero-shot generalization is an important capability, as it enables the model to generate images that are not explicitly seen during training. This has applications in areas such as image generation, image-to-image translation, and image-based question answering.

Liam, for example, might be able to generate an image of a cat based on the text "a fluffy white cat," even if the model has never seen an image of a cat before. Similarly, Sophia might be able to generate an image of a futuristic cityscape based on the text "a futuristic city on a distant planet," even if the model has never seen an image of a city on a distant planet before.

Overall, the definition of zero-shot generalization is a sensible one for text-to-image AIs, as it highlights the model's ability to generalize to new, unseen concepts and generate novel images.
